# JIT Code Generation with Nautilus and MLIR {#sec-nautilus-codegen}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: deepened 2026-05 against verified code"}
An earlier draft of this chapter described `nautilus::val<T>`
generically, without opening the real type. This draft is built
from a careful read of `nes-nautilus/include/Nautilus/DataTypes/VarVal.hpp`,
`Record.hpp/.cpp`, and the JIT boundary in
`nes-runtime/include/Pipelines/CompiledExecutablePipelineStage.hpp`.
Maintainer review is still recommended for Ch 12 specifically;
tracing-JIT explanations are unusually easy to get wrong.
:::

If you remember one thing about NebulaStream, remember this: it
JIT-compiles every query. There is no interpreter on the hot path
in production mode; there is no operator-by-operator dispatch; there
is no virtual function call between operators. The query becomes
native machine code, and the data flows through that code as fast
as the hardware can move it.

The framework that makes this happen is called Nautilus. It lives
in `nes-nautilus/`. This chapter is about how it works.

The mechanism is unusual enough that we will spend a few pages on
the *idea* before opening any code. Tracing JITs are common in
managed-runtime worlds (PyPy, V8) but rare in C++ database engines.
NebulaStream's choice to use one is the most consequential
architectural decision in the system, and it deserves the careful
introduction.

---

## 12.1 The problem: why interpret is too slow {#sec-interpret-slow}

Imagine an operator-tree interpreter for the simple query `SELECT
value FROM demo WHERE value > 0`. The interpreter, for each input
tuple, walks:

```
Source → next() → Selection → next() → Projection → next() → Sink
```

Each `next()` is a virtual function call. Between calls, the
interpreter has to box and unbox values, dispatch on their types,
check for nulls. The actual work — comparing `value` to `0` and
forwarding it — is a fraction of the cost. The rest is interpretation
overhead.

For OLTP this overhead is fine — a transaction touches a handful
of tuples and the overhead is negligible per query. For analytical
workloads over millions of tuples, the overhead is the bottleneck.
Hyper [@hyper-paper] established that compiling each query into a
native function eliminates the overhead and yields 10-100x speedups
on analytical workloads. Every modern analytical engine has followed
suit: Spark Catalyst, Flink Janino, ClickHouse, DuckDB, Arrow
Acero, Materialize all compile.

Stream engines need this for the same reason. A 1 MHz stream of
sensor readings is, over a day, 86 billion tuples. Saving 100 ns
per tuple in interpretation overhead saves 2.4 hours of CPU time.

---

## 12.2 Two approaches: AST emission vs. tracing {#sec-ast-vs-trace}

Once you have decided to compile, you have two broad choices:

**AST emission.** Each operator emits its own piece of IR (LLVM,
or some intermediate language) at compile time. The compiler
strings the operator-emitted pieces together. Each operator is, in
effect, a code generator that knows how to emit *itself*. This is
how Hyper, Umbra, and most database codegen frameworks work.

**Tracing.** Each operator is a *normal C++ class* whose `execute`
method is written as if to be interpreted. The framework runs the
operator once with special "tracing values" — values that record
every operation performed on them. The recorded operations form an
IR. The IR is compiled to native code.

The two approaches differ in where the smarts live. AST emission
puts the smarts in the operator: each operator knows how to emit
its own code. Tracing puts the smarts in the framework: operators
are just C++ that the framework records.

Tracing has a real ergonomic advantage. To add a new operator in
an AST-emission system, you write code that emits IR — a
significantly different mental model from writing code that does
the operation directly. To add a new operator in a tracing system,
you write code that does the operation, using the framework's
typed values. The tracing system records what you did and turns it
into IR for you.

NebulaStream's Nautilus framework uses tracing. This is, to my
knowledge, the only production-class C++ database engine that uses
tracing-based codegen. PyPy uses tracing; V8 uses tracing; but
neither is a database engine.

---

## 12.3 The Nautilus value type: nautilus::val<T> and VarVal {#sec-nautilus-val}

The unit of tracing is `nautilus::val<T>`, a type from the
external Nautilus library. Wherever an operator would naturally
use a `T` — a `uint64_t`, a `bool`, a pointer — it uses a
`nautilus::val<T>` instead. Operations on `nautilus::val<T>`
look like operations on `T` (the type provides the relevant
operator overloads), but each operation is recorded into a
trace.

Inside NebulaStream, the per-field value type is *not*
`nautilus::val<T>` directly — it is `VarVal`, a thin wrapper
defined in `nes-nautilus/include/Nautilus/DataTypes/VarVal.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-nautilus/include/Nautilus/DataTypes/VarVal.hpp
template <typename... T>
using var_val_helper =
    std::variant<VariableSizedData, nautilus::val<T>...>;

using var_val_t = var_val_helper<
    bool, uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t, uint64_t,
    int8_t, int16_t, int32_t, int64_t,
    float, double, char>;

class VarVal {
    detail::var_val_t value;
    nautilus::val<bool> null;
    bool nullable;
};
```

`VarVal` is a `std::variant` of `nautilus::val<T>` for every
primitive type in NebulaStream's type system (Chapter 3), plus
`VariableSizedData` for the VARSIZED escape, plus a tracing-aware
`null` flag and a compile-time `nullable` discriminator. The
choice of variant here is deliberate: at trace time, the
*concrete* type of a record field is known (the schema fixes
it), so each operator's read is a `std::get<nautilus::val<T>>`
rather than a runtime type dispatch.

Read a field: `record.read("value")` returns a `VarVal&`. Branch
on its value: the `> threshold` comparison is recorded by the
underlying `nautilus::val<T>::operator>`. Assign: `output.write("value", v)`
records a memory write.

To the operator author, the code reads like normal C++:

```cpp
void SelectionPhysicalOperator::execute(
    ExecutionContext& ctx, Record& record) const
{
    auto v = record.read(fieldName);
    if (v > nautilus::val<uint64_t>(threshold))
    {
        consumer->execute(ctx, record);
    }
}
```

To the framework, this is a sequence of trace operations: `read`,
`gt-const`, `if`, `recursive-execute`, `endif`. The framework
captures them, lowers to MLIR, and produces native code that
does exactly what the C++ said.

---

## 12.4 Trace-time vs. runtime constants {#sec-trace-time}

A subtlety the abbreviation glossary in `docs/frequently_used_abbreviations.md`
flags: there are *trace-time constants* and *runtime values*. A
trace-time constant is a value known when the trace runs — for
example, the threshold in a selection predicate is a constant set
at query compile time. A runtime value is a value known only when
the compiled code runs — for example, the field of an incoming
tuple.

Nautilus distinguishes the two. A trace-time constant is folded into
the generated code; a runtime value becomes a load. The author of an
operator does not have to think about which is which most of the
time, because the type system handles it: `nautilus::val<T>` is
runtime; a plain `T` (or a `nautilus::val<T>` constructed from a
trace-time constant) is constant-folded.

This is what allows a Selection to be expressed as `if (v >
threshold)` even though `threshold` differs per query: the
framework specialises the generated code for the specific
threshold.

---

## 12.5 The runtime data structures {#sec-runtime-structures}

JIT-friendly data structures matter because the JIT cannot inline
through a `std::unordered_map`'s virtual implementation. Nautilus
ships its own.

**`HashMap`.** Defined in
`nes-nautilus/include/Nautilus/Interface/HashMap/HashMap.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-nautilus/include/Nautilus/Interface/HashMap/HashMap.hpp
class HashMap {
public:
    virtual ~HashMap() = default;
    virtual AbstractHashMapEntry* insertEntry(
        HashFunction::HashValue::raw_type hash,
        AbstractBufferProvider* bufferProvider) = 0;
    [[nodiscard]] virtual uint64_t getNumberOfTuples() const = 0;
};
```

A small interface. The hash map is laid out across multiple buffers
(from the buffer manager), uses linear probing, and exposes a
single insertion point that the JIT can inline.

**`PagedVector`.** Defined in
`nes-nautilus/include/Nautilus/Interface/PagedVector/PagedVector.hpp`.
A dynamically-growing vector backed by a sequence of buffers, with
a cumulative-sum index for fast random access:

```cpp
struct PagedVector {
    struct TupleBufferWithCumulativeSum {
        explicit TupleBufferWithCumulativeSum(TupleBuffer buffer)
            : buffer(std::move(buffer)) { }
        size_t cumulativeSum{0};
        TupleBuffer buffer;
    };
    [[nodiscard]] const TupleBuffer* getTupleBufferForEntry(
        uint64_t entryPos) const;
};
```

`PagedVector` is used wherever an operator needs to accumulate an
unbounded sequence — the build side of a hash join's collision
chain, an aggregation's history of tuples per group. Like the
hash map, it is structured as a collection of `TupleBuffer`s
because that is what fits naturally with the buffer manager.

**`Record`.** We met this in Chapter 11. It is the per-tuple data
type; its operations (`read`, `write`) are the ones operators use
in their `execute` methods.

## 12.6 The compile pipeline {#sec-compile-pipeline}

The trace-to-native lowering happens in
`CompiledExecutablePipelineStage`
(`nes-runtime/include/Pipelines/CompiledExecutablePipelineStage.hpp`).
Its `compilePipeline()` method registers a lambda with the
Nautilus engine; the engine traces the lambda's execution and
produces a callable function pointer:

```cpp
// nes-runtime/include/Pipelines/CompiledExecutablePipelineStage.cpp (sketch)
nautilus::engine::CallableFunction<void, PipelineExecutionContext*,
                                   const TupleBuffer*, const Arena*>
CompiledExecutablePipelineStage::compilePipeline() const
{
    const std::function<void(
        nautilus::val<PipelineExecutionContext*>,
        nautilus::val<const TupleBuffer*>,
        nautilus::val<const Arena*>)> compiledFunction =
        [this](nautilus::val<PipelineExecutionContext*> pipelineCtx,
               nautilus::val<const TupleBuffer*> recordBufferRef,
               nautilus::val<const Arena*> arenaRef)
    {
        auto ctx = ExecutionContext(pipelineCtx, arenaRef);
        RecordBuffer recordBuffer(recordBufferRef);
        pipeline->getRootOperator().open(ctx, recordBuffer);
        // ... per-record loop, close, etc. ...
    };
    return engine.registerFunction(compiledFunction);
}
```

The `nautilus::val<…>` parameters tell the Nautilus engine
which arguments to trace; everything captured by `[this]` is
trace-time-constant. `engine.registerFunction` is the entry
point into the Nautilus library — it does the trace, lowers
to MLIR, and returns a callable.

`LowerToCompiledQueryPlanPhase` walks each pipeline and asks
for a compiled stage. The critical configuration:

```cpp
// nes-query-compiler/src/Phases/LowerToCompiledQueryPlanPhase.cpp
std::unique_ptr<ExecutablePipelineStage>
getStage(const std::shared_ptr<Pipeline>& pipeline)
{
    nautilus::engine::Options options;
    options.setOption("mlir.enableMultithreading", false);
    switch (pipelineQueryPlan->getExecutionMode())
    {
        case ExecutionMode::COMPILER:
            options.setOption("engine.Compilation", true);
            break;
        case ExecutionMode::INTERPRETER:
            options.setOption("engine.Compilation", false);
            break;
    }
    // ... construct ExecutablePipelineStage with MLIR/Nautilus backend
}
```

`ExecutionMode::COMPILER` lowers all the way to native and returns
a function pointer. `ExecutionMode::INTERPRETER` keeps the trace
in interpretable form and walks it for each tuple. Both produce
the *same* answer; the latter is much slower but, because the
trace is just data, much easier to debug.

The MLIR pipeline is multi-stage: `nautilus::ir` → `mlir-arith` →
`mlir-llvm` → `LLVM IR` → `native`. Each stage is a lowering pass
in the LLVM/MLIR sense [@mlir-paper]. The book will not walk
through the MLIR specifics; that is a topic large enough for its
own book.

---

## 12.7 What goes wrong, and how the engine is built to handle it {#sec-codegen-debug}

Code generation is the part of the engine where mistakes are
hardest to debug. A bug in a Selection is a wrong answer. A bug in
the codegen for a Selection is a wrong answer that depends on the
phase of the moon and the size of the alignment of an unrelated
struct.

NebulaStream defends against this in a few ways.

**INTERPRETER mode.** Flipping `execution_mode=INTERPRETER` runs
the same trace in the interpreter. If the answer differs from the
COMPILER answer, the bug is in the lowering, not in the operator
logic. We use this in essentially every reading exercise in this
book.

**Systests run in both modes.** The CI matrix includes runs with
and without compilation. A divergence between the two is caught
automatically.

**Trace dumps.** Setting `mlir.dumpIR` on the engine options
prints the MLIR for each compiled pipeline. For a one-operator
pipeline, the IR is a screenful; the human can usually spot
something obviously wrong.

**The Nautilus team owns the framework.** This is more
sociotechnical than technical, but it matters. Bugs in Nautilus
are reported to a small dedicated team that knows the lowering
pipeline; bugs in operators go to the operator team. The framework
boundary is also a debugging boundary.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how Hyper does this"}
Hyper [@hyper-paper], the academic predecessor of Tableau's
in-memory engine, was the first system to demonstrate the value of
per-query compilation. Hyper's approach is AST emission: each
operator emits LLVM IR directly through a builder API.

The operator code in Hyper looks very different from the
operator code in NebulaStream. Hyper's selection operator emits
IR; NebulaStream's selection operator does the actual operation
on `nautilus::val<T>`. For a developer, NebulaStream's tracing
approach is much closer to writing normal code. For a runtime,
the resulting native code is comparable.

The cost of tracing — and a real cost — is that the operator
must be expressible in the tracing language. Operations that
cannot be traced (e.g., a UDF written as a black-box function
pointer) require an "extern call" mechanism that is more awkward
than Hyper's "just call the function" model.
:::

---

## Summary {#sec-ch12-summary}

NebulaStream's Nautilus framework is a tracing JIT: operators are
written as normal C++ that uses `nautilus::val<T>` for runtime
values, and the framework records the operations into a trace,
lowers through MLIR to LLVM IR, and JIT-compiles to native code.
The runtime data structures (`HashMap`, `PagedVector`, `Record`)
are designed for the JIT's inlining requirements. The
`ExecutionMode::INTERPRETER` flag runs the trace as an
interpreter, which is much slower but invaluable for debugging.
The choice of tracing over AST emission is unusual for a C++
database engine and is the most consequential architectural
decision in NebulaStream.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch12-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 12.1: COMPILER vs INTERPRETER timing"}
Run a join systest in both modes:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1 \
    -- --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=COMPILER
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1 \
    -- --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER
```

Wall-clock time will differ by at least 10×. Verify that the
results are identical. The interpreter is your trace's source of
truth; the compiler is your trace's source of speed.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 12.2: dump the IR"}
For a small query, dump the MLIR. The flag is configurable
through the engine options. Identify the loop body. Identify
the trace-time constant (`> 0`) being folded. The IR for a
simple selection should fit on one screen.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 12.3: write a one-line operator"}
Sketch (no need to compile) a `MapPhysicalOperator` that
multiplies one field by a trace-time constant. The whole class
should be five lines of `execute`. Compare to the analogous
operator in a system you know — Spark Catalyst's, Flink's
Janino-emitted code. The brevity is the point.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 12.4: when tracing breaks down"}
Find a real or imagined operator that you would have a hard time
expressing through tracing — for example, an operator that calls
an external library function with side effects. How would you
shoehorn it into the framework? Hint: extern call mechanisms
exist; locate one and read its signature.
:::
